subtopic: REQUEST FOR ADJOURNMENT OF HOUSE ON NATIONAL HOLIDAY

speakeroldname: Hon. George A. Drew (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: REQUEST FOR ADJOURNMENT OF HOUSE ON NATIONAL HOLIDAY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege. Next Monday is the day set aside to honour the founding of our nation. It is a day which will be respected as a holiday in every city, town, village and other part of Canada. This house will be sitting for some time yet. No question of urgency arises which would necessitate sitting on such a day.
There are many hon. members who, as part of their duties as representatives of the people, will feel called upon to attend ceremonies in their own communities. For that reason I think it would be appropriate that we honour that day by adjourning when we adjourn on Friday until Tuesday next. I think this would be in keeping with the respect for the day marking the beginning of the history of a country which we all revere. I cannot imagine that on corresponding days in the United States or in other countries, where they respect the day set aside to mark the beginning of the nation, they would sit under these circumstances and deny to any of their members who have the opportunity to do so the right to participate in such celebrations as may take place.
It may well be that there are those who will not be able to attend the ceremonies in their own communities, but may I say to any of those who will not that there will be ceremonies here in Ottawa which will permit them to indicate their respect for the nation which is honoured on that day.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR ADJOURNMENT OF HOUSE ON NATIONAL HOLIDAY

subtopic: PURCHASE OF FEDERAL PROPERTY, JOYCEVILLE, ONT.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am glad to answer on behalf of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) starred question No. 55. The first question is:
1. Has the federal government completed its purchase of certain property or properties at Joyceville, Ontario, from Mr. Benjamin Franklin?
The answer is yes. Question No. 2 is:
2.	If so, how many acres were purchased from Mr. Franklin, and what is the total price paid, or to be paid, for the same?
The answer is 450 acres more or less. The price paid was $123,000, which was based on valuation of buildings at $83,000 and land at $40,000. Question No. 3 reads:
3.	What is the average price per acre of land in this area?
The answer is this. No average price is ascertainable, since prices depend on location, condition of land, state of buildings and similar factors. Question No. 4 is:
4.	Was the land purchased from Mr. Franklin clear of any encumbrances when negotiations for the purchase of the same were commenced?
The answer to this first part of the question is no. The second part of the question reads as follows:
If not, on what date was the land cleared of all encumbrances so that a sale to the government could be registered?
The answer is: On June 11, 1956, the crown acquired title to the property free of all encumbrances except three small executions amounting in all to $1,261.32 in respect of

which sufficient money was placed in trust to protect the crown. Question No. 5 is:
5.	Did the government purchase or agree to purchase from Mr. Franklin anything other than the land in question, such as stock or equipment? If so, how much was paid, or is to be paid, for the same?
The answer to both these questions is no.
Then question No. 6 reads:
To what purpose is (a) the land; (b) stock or other equipment, purchased from Mr. Franklin, to be put?
The answer to both parts of this question is as follows: Both the land and the stock will be used as site and for the construction and operation of a new penitentiary.
Then question No. 7 reads:
What are the names of any lawyers who acted or participated in any negotiations leading up to or relating to the sale of this property to the government, (a) on the part of Mr. Franklin; (b) on the part of the government?
The answer is that the lawyers who acted on behalf of Mr. Franklin were Messrs. Arnoldi, Parry and Campbell of Toronto; and on behalf of the government Messrs. Gibson, Sands and Flanigan of Kingston.

speechtext: I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Fisheries, notice of which was sent to his office yesterday. Is the minister aware of the reports that have been made about unwarranted destruction of salmon by the spraying of forests in New Brunswick and more particularly spraying at or near a salmon hatchery where a large number of young salmon were destroyed? If so, what action is being taken to prevent a repetition of such occurrences?

subtopic: NEW BRUNSWICK
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member gave me notice of his question in sufficient time to wire our scientists and to get a report. On Saturday, June 9, commercial planes spraying D.D.T. over the forests between the Northwest and Southwest Miramichi rivers crossed over the hatchery area of Miramichi hatchery. Definite oil slicks appeared on the pond and in the hatchery, and during the following week over 800,000 salmon and trout were destroyed. The fisheries scientists are well aware of the need for spruce bud-worm spraying and have tried to work out a program with the operators so that the hatchery areas will not be sprayed. The plans given to our scientists this spring showed that this hatchery area was not to be sprayed. This is the third such occurrence and this time we lost one-third of our hatchery stock and we are now examining the possibility of taking legal action against the firm concerned.

maintopic: STATEMENT RESPECTING MAINTENANCE OF FLOOR PRICE

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Gardiner (Minister of Agriculture):
maintopic: STATEMENT RESPECTING MAINTENANCE OF FLOOR PRICE
speechtext:
Before the orders of the day are proceeded with, I should like to answer a question asked by the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe) on June 22. In my absence he put the question to the Minister of Trade and Commerce and the minister said:
Since my hon. friend has directed the question to me, I shall answer it.
Then he went on to say:
I shall draw it to the attention of the Minister of Agriculture. I expect he will be back in his seat next week.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce has brought this matter to my attention.

maintopic: STATEMENT RESPECTING MAINTENANCE OF FLOOR PRICE
speechtext: Now that you are back.

maintopic: STATEMENT RESPECTING MAINTENANCE OF FLOOR PRICE
speechtext:
Now that I am back, yes; and now that we are both back. The question was a follow-up on some questioning by different members that had been asked the previous two days. The first question itself is in these words:
In view of the uncertainty left in the minds of both producers and consumers of butter by the answers given the other day by the parliamentary assistant with regard to the sale of 25 million pounds of butter at 2 cents per pound less than the cost to the government, what security has the butter producer that the floor price of 58 cents per pound will be maintained throughout June, July and August, the months during which I understand the delivery of the 25 million pounds is to be made?
The security is that the agricultural prices support board of the Department of Agriculture offers 58 cents a pound basis Toronto and Montreal and 57 -cents a pound basis

Inquiries of the Ministry Vancouver on the markets right across Canada every day, and no one is required to sell grade A butter at less than 58 cents, so that the price is secured in that way. The second question continued:
If the floor price is 58 cents and the government only buys about one-third of what the dairy producer produces, then what assurance has the producer that the 56 cents, which is the price at which the government is selling butter into the trade-a greater amount at 56 cents than they are buying at 58 cents-with no particular quality distinction-
The position in relation to that is, as I will show in a minute by reading the order in council, that the quality distinction in respect of the butter that the agricultural prices support board is dealing with is that it is grade A butter, all of it, that is being dealt with. The matter of the 56 cents is, I think, dealt with in the answer to the third question which was:
-and also what assurance has the consumer whether the consumer price is to be based on the 58 cents the government is paying for the butter or the 56 cents at which it is selling a larger amount?
The fact is that both actions are based upon 58 cents. In the first place, the 58 cents is always available for fresh butter coming on the market, and in determining the 56 cents at which butter was sold to the trade it was estimated-as a matter of fact, it was actually figured-that butter could not be sold by the trade at much less than 58 cents if they were going to make the usual profits in selling that butter. The cost of switching it from bulk butter to prints and putting it on the market is sufficient to take up the greater part of the difference between the 56 cents and the 58 cents, so that the 58 cents pretty well governs no matter whether it is the consumer or the producer who is affected by it. Fresh butter is available at 58 cents per pound and 1955 butter may be available at slightly less. I continue with question four:
I might also ask the Minister of Trade and Commerce to have the minister or his assistant tell us whether it is a fact that 5 million pounds of this butter has been sold in western Canada at a further reduction to the trade of 2 cents additional, with no assurance to the consumer or the producer.
The fact is, as I understand the situation at the moment, that no such sale has actually been made, but I suppose it could be estimated that the order in council itself governs the price to the extent that in some places the price obtained by the individual might be less than the basic price over a certain area, and I think I should read the order in council to make that clear:
Whereas under authority of paragraph (b) of subsection (1) of section 9 of the Agricultural Prices Support Act, 1944, the agricultural prices


support board proposes to offer to purchase from May 1, 1956 to April 30, 1958, Canada first grade creamery butter-
Because we do not deal with any other, -and under authority of paragraph (a) of subsection (1) of section 9 of the said act proposes to prescribe the following prices therefor:
58 cents per pound basis delivery Halifax, Saint John, Montreal and Toronto,
57 cents per pound basis delivery Vancouver, all purchases to be subject to such terms and conditions as may be specified by the agricultural prices support board.
Therefore, His Excellency the Governor General in Council, on the recommendation of the Minister of Agriculture and under authority of paragraph (a) of section 2 of the Agricultural Prices Support Act, 1944, is pleased to designate and doth hereby designate as an agricultural product for the purposes of the said act, Canada first grade creamery butter . . .
With regard to this last question, I would point out that the places at which butter would be delivered at the floor price, Halifax, Saint John, Montreal, Toronto and Vancouver, are on the two sides of the prairie section of Canada. Butter goes west to Vancouver from Alberta and probably part of Saskatchewan. Butter goes east from Saskatchewan and Manitoba to the eastern market. Of course, the cost of moving butter from the prairies to either one of these markets is accounted for and it would be somewhere between 1 and 2 cents, and the butter will of course be sold under contracts, whether it is to the government or whoever it may be, at a lower price than it is sold at the two ends of Canada.
I would not be definite in saying that it is below the 57-cent price in certain sections of the west if the butter is coming east but it certainly would be lower than these set prices. I should like to point this out though, while I am dealing with the matter, and I suppose this is the question which is in the minds of some. The fact is that the 56-cent price at which the butter has been offered to the trade is 2 cents below the 58-cent price at which it was purchased last year. It is 1955 butter. In the first year that this plan was followed, two years ago, 2J cents a pound was the difference. Last year it was 2 cents a pound. Last year we permitted the trade to buy butter at 56 cents during all the time the plan was in operation and the plan was in operation down until September. This year we decided that, in the interests of the producer-and, we think, in the interests of the consumer too-it was preferable that the trade should take delivery of as much butter as possible as early as possible. So we made a definite arrangement with them that they would take 25 million pounds, a large part of it-about a third of it-by June 15; probably another one-third by July 15 and another one-third by August

15. The matter of the cost of carrying butter under this plan would not be as great to the agricultural prices support board as it was under the plans followed in the previous two years. That was the reason for entering into the arrangement which we have entered into for this year.
Then there was the additional fact that every time we talked about marketing butter anywhere outside of Canada during this last six months or eight months, someone in the house somewhere-usually on the opposition side-suggested that butter ought, as far as possible, to be sold in Canada at any lower price at which it was going to be sold. We therefore thought that the arrangement made was such that probably more of the butter which we may have for sale would be sold and consumed within Canada on this basis than on the other. So we are proceeding to have it done in that way because of that desire. I think the policy will work out to the benefit of both the producer and the consumer.

maintopic: STATEMENT RESPECTING MAINTENANCE OF FLOOR PRICE
speechtext: In view of the statement made by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) may I ask him this question. He said that they are selling butter to the trade at 56 cents and are only buying one-third of what the producer produces during these three months. Is that not giving effect to reducing the price to the producer by at least 2 cents to 56 cents? If they can buy from you at 56 cents, what is to hinder them from buying from the producer at 56 cents, 2 cents below the floor price?

maintopic: STATEMENT RESPECTING MAINTENANCE OF FLOOR PRICE
speechtext: No. We do not think so.

maintopic: STATEMENT RESPECTING MAINTENANCE OF FLOOR PRICE
speechtext: You buy only one-third.

maintopic: STATEMENT RESPECTING MAINTENANCE OF FLOOR PRICE
speechtext: Every day the price for that fresh butter is 58 cents.

maintopic: STATEMENT RESPECTING MAINTENANCE OF FLOOR PRICE
speechtext: For how much?

maintopic: STATEMENT RESPECTING MAINTENANCE OF FLOOR PRICE
speechtext: For whatever they offer.

maintopic: STATEMENT RESPECTING MAINTENANCE OF FLOOR PRICE
speechtext: You took only one-third last year.

maintopic: STATEMENT RESPECTING MAINTENANCE OF FLOOR PRICE
speechtext:
If we took one-third last year it worked out that way. Some years it worked out less than that and some years more than that. One year we scarcely got any. The producer can always deliver his butter-that is grade "A" butter-to the board at 58 cents if no one offers 58 or more. He can sell it every day and every hour that the markets are open at that price.
On the other question-I just referred to it but perhaps I should have made it plainer- may I say this. As to the 56 cents, the price that the trade is going to charge for the butter will naturally be very close to the 58 cents-that is for the 1955 butter-because
Inquiries of the Ministry they have to convert solids into prints or forms of one kind and another in order to sell it to the retail trade. By the time they have done that, they cannot afford to sell the butter at less than about 58 cents. So an attempt is made to have all the butter that is going into the market at as close as possible to the 58 cents paid to the producer. We think it is working closely enough that there is not going to be any undue advantage to the trade over and above what one would naturally expect the trade to get in that kind of deal. When it is all worked out, I think you will find that neither the producer nor the consumer suffers by it. The quantity is only beneficial to us in the fact that the more the trade takes from us, the better we are pleased. We simply have to carry it over until the trade wants it again and pay the carrying charges. If the policy works out in the manner in which we hope it will work out we will save on carrying charges compared with previous years.

subtopic: COLUMBIA RIVER
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, before I continue the remarks which I had commenced last evening, I should like to apologize to Your Honour for an inaccurate answer I gave to Your Honour when you asked me, after I moved the adjournment of the debate, whether a report from the standing committee on external affairs from which I had quoted had been reported to the house. I answered that it had. Unfortunately, that answer was wrong. Although the report in question has been distributed, the committee has not made a formal report to the house. I trust that no harm has been done. All of these reports from the standing committees are distributed at once and the members had the report. Furthermore, there have been quite extensive reports in the press of the statement by General McNaugh-ton which I quoted. As a matter of fact, I had intended to quote from a press dispatch -it would probably have been more in order-rather than from the committee's proceedings.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: COLUMBIA RIVER
speechtext: May I tell the hon. gentleman that I am always very sympathetic to those who admit they are wrong.

subtopic: COLUMBIA RIVER
speechtext:
I had pointed out last evening, Mr. Speaker, that a week from today the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Lesage) is to hold a conference with the premier of British Columbia in Victoria at which the problems arising out of the development of the Columbia river for power purposes and similar questions will be discussed. I had stressed the view of the official opposition that it is essential there should be the closest co-operation between the two governments on these questions, which I admit at once are difficult ones.
Then, I was going on to point out that there had been developments within the last few weeks which should be drawn to the attention of the house. They have to do primarily with the manner in which the dam and the power plant are to be constructed at Mica creek on the Big Bend of the Columbia river. I am quite sure that the minister will agree


with me when I say that the Mica creek development is the key to the development of the whole of the Columbia river in Canada. This view is held by the minister's own officials, the provincial government officials and by the United States. I have here a report made by Senator Richard L. Neuberger of Oregon, to the Senate committee on interior and insular affairs as a result of his investigation last fall. He had this to say:
But Mica is the key to the development of the Columbia river in Canada.
He also said, confirming the opinions of dominion and provincial authorities:
And Mica is ready for construction in the immediate future.
Both of those statements are accurate. I explained last night that General McNaughton had taken the position on June 14 that someone could go ahead right away and make final plans for the Mica creek project. The following day there was a press report of the reaction of the premier of British Columbia to that statement by General McNaughton. I am quoting from the Vancouver Sun of June 15, which states:
Asked to comment on a statement in Ottawa by General A. G. L. McNaughton, Chairman of the Canadian section of the International Joint Commission, that engineers have deemed such a project feasible, premier Bennett said:
"There has never been any doubt about the feasibility of this dam.'*
"The Social Credit government of B.C. has always been in favour of the Mica creek dam. We've said all along that it was feasible."
He also said:
The premier told a reporter he has made no definite plans as yet concerning construction of the power station.
Then, there is this further interesting paragraph in quotation marks:
"'If it hadn't been for the interference from Ottawa, we in B.C. would already have the dam under construction."
The next day, June 16-

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
subtopic: COLUMBIA RIVER
speechtext: You do not believe that.

subtopic: COLUMBIA RIVER
speechtext:
I am not saying what I believe at the moment. The following day a dispatch appeared in the Vancouver Province reporting that the B.C. Electric, which is the power company on the lower mainland of British Columbia, was seeking authority to build the Mica creek project at a cost of $247 million as estimated by General McNaughton. This was the first time that news had broken; it was something new in the picture. The dispatch contains two interesting paragraphs. The first one is this:
Before work can begin, there must be agreement between Ottawa and Victoria on the development at Mica, 80 miles north of Revelstoke.

That, of course, is an accurate statement of fact, that there must be agreement between the two governmental bodies. Then it went on:
An understanding also is important between Ottawa and Washington on downstream benefits on the stretches of the Columbia in American
territory.
That, too, is accurate, and those are the two vital factors to be remembered in this whole question. May I diverge for a moment to deal with this question of downstream benefits. As Your Honour knows, what is meant by downstream benefits is that the plant downstream which benefits by dams upstream and thereby can produce more power, should pay something for that situation. Canada has taken the position that payment must be in power rather than in money. The Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent), when he conferred with President Eisenhower in April of this year, apparently did briefly discuss this question of the Columbia river. Then, on May 23 the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources made the statement that these officials in the higher brackets in Canada and the United States would be conferring about the whole question.
While there is great urgency about settling this problem of downstream benefits, it is obvious that nothing much can be done until the fall. I do suggest to the minister in this connection that it would be well for him to have a top level official of the British Columbia government sit in with him or with whatever other Canadian federal minister participates in the talks, because British Columbia is the province most widely affected at the present time. I think it would further co-operation if an arrangement of that kind could be made.
The B.C. Electric statement was made on June 16. Then, on June 21 Premier Bennett made a statement dealing with the proposal that the B.C. Electric should develop this project. He made it quite clear that he was hoping to have United States interests build that dam. I think he obviously intended the power plant would be built by Canadians, whether by the B.C. Power Commission or by private Canadians, he did not say; but he did indicate that he thought the best way to build the dam would be to have it done by United States interests, and he puts up quite a reasonable argument in favour of that proposal.
The dispatch reads as follows:
If power is to be developed on the Columbia, said the premier, then the cost must be kept low.
And, he said, U.S. financing of the dam would mean that this cost would not be charged against the electricity generated at the dam site.
In effect, the 20 per cent "cream"-
7. 1958	5437
Columbia River-Power Development
He has in mind that the United States should pay in the nature of 20 per cent of the additional power produced for downstream benefits.
-from the extra generation on the U.S. side would come to B.C. at a next to nothing cost.
He believes, and evidently sincerely believes, that United States interests are willing to build that dam without asking for any return, other than the fact that they will get more water through their plants in times when the Columbia river is low. The premier thinks that Canada and British Columbia, of course, will save that much money and therefore the users of the power will get it that much cheaper. The following day he was reported as having amplified his statement as follows:
The premier reiterated that he felt the downstream benefits would make it worth while for the United States to finance construction of Mica dam through formation of Canadian companies.
Then he is quoted verbatim:
We want to make sure the dams are paid for by the downstream benefits, that we get all the power at the dams, and that we get a minimum of 20 per cent of the extra power created downstream on the American side.
There is no room for middlemen in this hydro electric. The most likely development will be by large users of power on both sides of the border.
Now, of course, when he suggests the figure of 20 per cent for downstream benefits, that undercuts the negotiations that the dominion might undertake with the United States government on this very question of payment for downstream benefits.
The premier of British Columbia has taken the same stand before. He took it in May, and then his minister, Mr. Sommers, made a similar statement in the British Columbia legislature in February. It would appear certain they are hoping that the Americans will build this dam free and that someone in Canada can then go in and build the power plant. There is some reason for his contention, because I quote again from Senator Neuberger's report to the United States senate committee. Senator Neuberger had this to say with regard to the Mica creek project:
A second specific proposal is the offer of the Puget Sound Utilities Council to finance the construction of Mica dam, also in return for a share of the downstream power benefits realized by Bonneville power administration as a result of the storage provided by the huge Mica reservoir. This proposal was explained to me in Seattle by Dr. Paul J. Raver, former Bonneville power administrator who now heads Seattle City Light and is chairman of the Puget Sound Utilities Council, and Mr. Jack D. Stevens, consulting engineer for the Council.
The Puget Sound Utilities Council is composed of the Seattle and Tacoma city light systems, public utility districts of Snohomish and Chelan counties, Washington, and the Puget Sound Power and Light Company. Together, these five
5438	HOUSE OF
Columbia River-Power Development utilities propose to finance construction of the Mica project at an estimated cost of $250 million. Ownership of the project would then be turned over to British Columbia, which could arrange for the installation of at-site power. Storage from the Mica reservoir would be released to increase prime power at Columbia river plants in the United States now in existence or under construction by 1,100,000 kilowatts.
There would be that great increase in production in the United States by reason of the Mica dam. I continue:
Of this increase, the members of the Puget Sound Utilities Council would receive from Bonneville power administration the amount of power necessary to amortize the council's costs of financing the Mica project-estimated at about 800,000 kilowatts. The remaining 300,000 kilowatts would be added to B.P.A.'s power pool.
Then, the senator went on:
This plan has been proposed to officials of the Canadian government, of the government of British Columbia, and of Bonneville power administration. Like the Kaiser proposal, it depends on agreement with all three of these governmental authorities.
Incidentally, I believe that if a scheme of that kind were adopted the United States federal treasury, directly or indirectly, would be helping to finance that Mica creek scheme. Frankly, I am a little doubtful of the Americans being willing to put up $250 million for nothing, without being pretty sure that they get adequate compensation in one way or another.
However, these facts I have mentioned indicate that today there is great urgency to get this problem settled as between the federal government and the government of British Columbia. I hope the minister has something to offer to the premier of British Columbia in this conference and I hope that today the minister will give us some indication of the policy of the dominion government on this question. There certainly has been no clear-cut statement from the dominion as yet as to what this government is prepared to do.
Mind you, Mr. Speaker, last year this government took a licensing power over installations on the Columbia river; in fact, it took a veto power so that any project brought forward by the province of British Columbia, or anyone else, can be vetoed here under the act of last year. The Vancouver Sun summed that up very neatly on June 15 when it said:
In bringing up this "completely firm proposal" by his engineers for Mica creek, General McNaughton provides a positive policy to set beside the negative, but vital, role played by Ottawa last year when it stopped the British Columbia government's plan to sell British Columbia water rights to United States industry at give-away prices.
It would be unfair for the federal government to sit back and exercise a veto and to


say, "Here, you cannot do this and you cannot do that" without making any suggestion. There is a responsibility on the Canadian government to make its position perfectly clear and then do what it can to help. For example, what is the policy of this government on the question of United States control or United States participation in the Mica creek project? That has never been made clear. Personally, I have never hesitated to take the position that I believe this project should be undertaken by Canadians and for Canadians, particularly because all the rest of the development on the river depends on what is done at Mica creek. The Mica creek project will set the pattern for the whole river, and at least a billion dollars will be involved when the over-all plan has been completed.
Then, is the dominion government willing to give any help with the financing? It seems to me that is the way in which the dominion government can step into this picture. I do not believe there would be one cent lost if the dominion government placed its moneyraising power behind the provincial government. The dominion can raise money at a cheaper rate than the provinces. We have now got to the position in this country where, in the case of public utilities of this type, the dominion I believe must help underwrite the financing. The same is true on the Saint John river in New Brunswick. On the Columbia the dominion government can very well help the province of British Columbia, with the result that that dam could be built at a lower rate, power would be cheaper, and Canadians could do the whole thing. I place that proposal before the government with all the earnestness of which I am capable. I asked the minister about it on March 20. At page 2298 of Hansard I said:
Is the government prepared to negotiate on the basis of a joint investment program?
The minister replied:
Mr. Speaker, I have no comment to add at this time.
I believe the time is here when the minister can say whether the dominion is willing to co-operate on this basis to help out, or on any other basis. Above all, co-operation between the two governments is vital. If they go on sniping at each other from the distance of 3,000 miles, as they have been doing now off and on for many months, the Columbia river will never be adequately developed as it would otherwise be, and the people of British Columbia and, in the long run, the people of Canada will be the sufferers.
This scheme is the largest potential scheme there has ever been in British Columbia. I pointed out to Your Honour that the total

Columbia River-Power Development
cost of the developments on the river alone would be at least a billion dollars. In addition, there will be as much more spent on transmission lines and on facilities for distributing the power. In the end, it may mean an increase in the population of British Columbia of a million or 2 million people. No one knows just exactly how much it would mean. The possibilities are staggering; it is the greatest thing that has ever appeared over the horizon in the west coast province.
Because of these facts I feel it has been wise today to take the time of the house to bring up this question at this particular stage. I hope that when the minister goes to Victoria next week he will do his part to bury the hatchet-not to try to bury it in the premier's skull but simply to bury the hatchet-and if that attitude is adopted the result will probably be that the two governments will be able to co-operate and get on with some reasonable plan for the development of this Mica creek project by Canadians and for Canadians.

subtopic: COLUMBIA RIVER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green) has made quite a comprehensive review of the Columbia basin development situation with particular reference to Mica creek. I do not intend to take the time of the house to repeat a great deal of what he has had to say but I do want to present to the house and particularly to the minister the point of view of this group on this very important question. Before doing that, Mr. Speaker, I might say that sitting here listening to the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra I was thinking of 1915, 1916 and 1917 when we manned the trenches in France together and spent a good many wet nights and weeks in various trenches there fighting a common enemy and trying to achieve a common objective. I think we are doing that here today. I was thinking we belonged to a battalion that was in the habit of obtaining its objectives and I trust that is a good omen when we come to discuss this situation together; and more than that, Mr. Speaker, we are both very happy to know that one of our comrades whom we have not seen since 1919 is here to witness another attack on an objective that is of importance to the Canadian people by members of his old battalion.
This conference in Victoria between the premier of British Columbia and the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Lesage) concerning the development of the Columbia river is one of prime importance, as the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra said, to the people of our province. I have been a resident of the Columbia river
basin for 50 years and I have fully appreciated the intense concern and interest that has been shown throughout the whole district. In fact, I think Senator Neuberger mentioned it in his report, the alertness of the whole population to what this development means to that area and to British Columbia as a whole. We do hope that this first conference between the minister and the premier of British Columbia is a definite step toward one of the greatest developments in hydro that will occur in Canada. As never before, public attention is focused on this forthcoming conference in British Columbia. I have had letters from newspaper people, from a good many people throughout my own constituency and from a great many points in southern British Columbia. While in some cases the letters are written mainly on other topics, during the last month there have been written to me many letters in which people have made some reference to this forthcoming conference and expressed the hope that something fruitful would result from it.
Both governments, the federal and provincial, have a great responsibility to the people of British Columbia and to the people of Canada in this matter. If this responsibility is to be met, we in this group maintain that three things are essential and I mention them so that the minister will be well informed as to the position of this group with respect to this great projected development.
The first thing we say is necessary is a spirit of co-operation between the government of Canada and the government of British Columbia. This thing is too big for party politics to enter. The future success of these developments will be determined by how big the personalities involved are on these occasions.
The second requirement for success in our opinion is the establishment for some type of Columbia basin authority either by the provincial government under the public power commission or as a result of the cooperation between the federal and provincial governments. If the entire water resources of the area are to be developed to the advantage of the people as a whole, in our opinion there will have to be some government authority, some control, some planning, some regulation and some logical approach to the development of the water resources in relation to the development of the forest resources, the mineral resources and the land resources.
When it comes to suggesting an authority such as the Tennessee valley authority or the great public developments on the Columbia river south of the line, I think the record
5440	HOUSE OF
Columbia River-Power Development clearly proves the great advantages of a planned development under public ownership or public control. I think anyone who has studied this question will admit the record proves that public control and planning provide certain things that are not possible under any other form of development.
First of all they provide for the scientific development of the water resources in question. They provide for low cost power such as we have demonstrated in the Tennessee valley development and in the United States public developments south of the line on the Columbia where we have the cheapest power on the North American continent. They also provide for a co-ordinated expansion of industry and agriculture, and to assist that expansion of industry a fair distribution of the power for industrial purposes and a fair and proper use of the available water for irrigation purposes. They also provide that water resources are developed to the public advantage without the waste that would occur through piecemeal development of a basin such as this. All these things, then, bring the consequent economic improvement and also the human welfare for millions that results from that improvement.
The third thing we in this group say is necessary-and I think we in this group are not alone in feeling this way; I am quite sure the great bulk of the people of British Columbia, and particularly in the southeastern portion of British Columbia, share our view-is that action should be taken as soon as possible to implement what has been a dream for 50 years on the part of some people. We feel this action is necessary if we are going to take advantage of these resources at a time when they will be urgently needed.
The development of the basin has been the subject of discussion for many years in the Kootenay country in a general way without information. There were men, X remember 45 or 50 years ago, who could look forward and see the great possibilities for the development of the hydro resources of the area. I suppose the first general consideration of the problem occurred at the time of the 1944 Columbia reference to this house and to congress in Washington. I think that reference came about because of the realization on the part of those who were in this government at that time that the great development south of the line would soon mean the necessity for the development of our resources north of the line.
I pay a tribute to the farsightedness of those who worked for that reference to this house and to congress in 1944. At that time there were some people who thought that


that was rather far-fetched, but the fact is that that reference was the first time that public attention was directed to the possibility of development in the basin. Since that time we have had twelve years of investigation, largely at the expense of the federal government. I think all Canadians who have been interested in this problem recognize the great contribution which General McNaugh-ton has made to this investigation. We recognize his concern over the problem and to make certain that Canadian interests are protected and his farsighted and continuous application to the many aspects of this development.
We appreciate also the interest the minister has shown and his attention to the many unusual aspects of this question. I know personally that the minister is intensely interested in this development and has given a great deal of his time to a study of the situation. He has taken an active part in the development of public policy in this respect.
I think some tribute should be paid to the engineering staff of the water resources branch of the minister's department, the Department of Public Works and the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys. There have been some excellent men who have worked behind the scenes at most modest salaries compared with what some of them could get in private industry because they are interested in the development of water resources for Canadians. When I think of these men working behind the scenes and doing a lot of most technical work and applying their minds to the problem over a period of twelve years, I am always reminded of two lines in Gray's "Elegy in a Country Churchyard" as follows:
Full many a flower is born to blush unseen,
And waste its sweetness on the desert air.
I feel that many of those men who worked behind the scenes do not get sufficient recognition. In some quarters there is a tendency to look upon civil servants as being people who are simply seeking security and who are anxious to earn a living with as little effort as possible. Civil servants as a group are human beings like us in this house and have the failings of human beings. I know of a good many civil servants of Canada whose contributions to the welfare of this country are unheard of, unsung and almost unknown. I think this is something that should be said because of the good work these people do.
The result of the reference and twelve years of investigation was climaxed I think by General McNaughton's announcement to the committee on external affairs recently

that Mica creek was a positive plan which could be proceeded with. That was the first definite announcement of any large-scale development in the area. It represents a positive approach. Last year the government had to take a negative approach to protect the water resources on behalf of the people of British Columbia and on behalf of the people of Canada, and I think rightly so. I supported them in that effort.
As the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green) has indicated, this announcement created a great deal of interest in British Columbia and has served to focus attention directly on the Mica creek dam which would be located geographically to act as a hub for the distribution of power over the whole southern half of British Columbia. This is a development which the general told us will cost about $274 million and will produce up to 1,100,000 kilowatts.
After twelve years of investigation we have sufficient information for the planning to commence and to unfold. This is the dawn of the day for which a good many people in our province have been longing. In the past the government did its duty by making the reference; the engineers and technicians have done their duty by producing the facts; the Creator provided the natural resources in abundance, and what happens from this time on will depend upon the capacity of this government and the government of British Columbia to meet their responsibilities to the people of this country.
The development of the water resources of the Columbia river basin in Canada should bring untold blessings to millions of people in days to come. From the point of view of this group it is the responsibility of the governments concerned to make sure that these natural resources will be utilized to the advantage of those millions of Canadians.
Some reference was made by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra to a statement from the minister prior to his leaving for Vancouver. I must say that I do not agree with that suggestion. I do not think it would be fair to ask the minister to make a statement in this house with respect to this question just before he is to meet the premier of British Columbia and carry on discussions and negotiations in Victoria. I can well understand his not being willing to do that at this particular time. I hope that in the days to come we shall have an announcement of government policy in clear terms. We in this group wish the minister every success in his trip to Victoria and in all he undertakes in connection with this great development which should be to the general advantage of the Canadian people.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased that the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green) has raised this most important question at a time when the minister is preparing to go to British Columbia to discuss the Columbia river basin development. I certainly do not agree with the statement that it was federal government interference which delayed the development of the Mica creek. Undoubtedly the Columbia valley reference delayed some of the undertakings which might have taken place and which would have been of tremendous benefit to the United States only. With that contention I can wholeheartedly agree.
It is quite obvious, as the hon. member has pointed out, that this long-range sniping is not going to get us anywhere. To me it is quite obvious that the sniping has been from the one direction, from the west to the east, since this debate was concluded last year and the international rivers bill brought into being.
If this matter were one entirely of economics I would be in complete agreement with the submission that nothing should be done to develop either the Kootenay or the Columbia valley until we have absolute engineering data to prove that the Columbia can be diverted economically and feasibly into the Fraser river. There are already many political developments, and when I say "political", I mean developments which show that any such diversion would affect many thousands of people. For that reason it would require provincial legislation which might be held up for many years. The federal Department of Fisheries has gone along with the premier of British Columbia in saying that there shall be no diversion of the Columbia river into the Fraser until absolute assurance has been given that no fisheries will be destroyed. For that reason I am quite sure it would be quite a number of years before an official decision would be made on the diversion of the Columbia into the Fraser.
On the other hand I think there will be perhaps less difficulty in determining the feasibility of the diversion of the Kootenay into the Columbia river. This, however, would dislocate a large number of people in East Kootenay, would cause a great deal of hardship and would put under water very large tracts of land that have become well known as great farming communities and tourist resorts. I think that the opinion of the people of East Kootenay, and perhaps of the entire southeastern portion of British Columbia, is that this diversion should be avoided if at all possible.

Columbia River-Power Development I have a resolution here from the associated boards of trade and chambers of commerce of southeastern British Columbia which reads in part as follows:
Whereas the proposed diversion of international waters in the Columbia river system is inconsistent with the spirit and terms of the said reference, adversely affecting rapid and rational development plans and good international relations, and Whereas in the development of the hydro power resources of the watershed, the free interchange of surplus electric energy is a factor of great economic importance . . .
I do not agree with the chambers of commerce that the diversion of either the Kootenay or the Columbia entirely within Canada is, as they say, inconsistent with the spirit and terms of the said Columbia basin reference. That has become the opinion of some of the leading experts on water power in British Columbia, but in my opinion it just is not so. The reference is quite defined, and certainly the boundary waters treaty of 1909 is entirely consistent with the views held by the federal government.
However, we have seen newspaper reports indicating that the British Columbia Power Corporation is prepared to proceed with a dam at Mica creek, but in announcing that determination they make no reference whatsoever to diversion of the Kootenay river into the Columbia. It appears that it has been determined that the project would be economic without the diversion of the headwaters of the Kootenay river, and therefore that is unessential to the plan. It has also been pointed out that the Mica dam might be built by Canadian corporations or by Canadian governments without jeopardizing the plan for the diversion of the Columbia into the Fraser. The Mica dam would be essential in any case and the water would be diverted some miles below the dam.
I think we are entitled to consider these two basins as separate entities. That contention is put forward by the chambers of commerce, and in this connection I find myself in agreement with them to some extent. In this regard I should like to refer again to the resolution which has this to say:

There is another matter that it seems to me has been overlooked, or perhaps not overlooked but not given enough emphasis. That is the question of integrating the Pend d'Oreille system with the Kootenay system. The Pend d'Oreille system, of course, in the United States is used almost entirely for storage in the lower Columbia. The Pend d'Oreille river enters Canada near Waneta and flows through Canada about 14 miles. There is no storage whatever on the Pend d'Oreille in Canada. There is, however, 54 million acre feet annually stored on the Pend d'Oreille for the purposes I have previously stated.
Having regard to this situation, a power site was installed on the Pend d'Oreille by the West Kootenay Power Company at Waneta just before it enters the Columbia river. This dam cost between $30 million and $35 million and is making as much use as it can of the storage on the Pend d'Oreille in the United States. However, as I said earlier, that storage is released purely for the purpose of supplying a constant flow for the Bonneville and Grand Coulee power installations and so on down the line in the United States. For that reason the flow is extremely erratic. I believe it fluctuates between 4,000 cubic feet per second up to
36.000	cubic feet per second. Hence you can see that it is not possible to make the best use of that water. There are many days on which it flows over the spillway and is a complete waste.
The installations at Waneta at the present time can make use of 12,000 cubic feet per second, and of course there are times when they have available only 4,000 cubic feet per second. If the water from the Pend d'Oreille storage could be regulated to a mean flow, they could be provided with about
24.000	cubic feet per second, which would permit doubling the installation and doubling the output of that plant. One can realize that a plant that cost $35 million produces a fairly large amount of electricity. I believe it could produce somewhere near the amount that is already being produced in the lower Kootenay.
What would be required before this regulation of the flow from the Pend d'Oreille could be accomplished would be an integration of the West Kootenay Power Corporation system and the Bonneville Power corporation who I believe are responsible for the administration of the power that is produced at Grand Coulee. A power line joining these

Columbia River-Power Development two systems would have the effect of integrating the entire system. Then the water releases from the Pend d'Oreille would be integrated with the water releases from the Kootenay and would maintain a constant flow. The turbines would be turning at all times. There would be no wastage of the stored water, and there would be available at certain periods of the year a flow of electricity to the south, while at other times of the year there would be a flow of electricity back into Canada. It simply means that until the energy and the flow of these systems have been integrated, there cannot be a complete and proper development of the Kootenay system.
I think the minister should keep that question in mind and to the forefront when he is discussing the whole matter with the premier of the province of British Columbia. If it is true that the diversion of the Columbia river into the Fraser river would be feasible only if it obtained the flood waters or the headwaters of the Kootenay, then I certainly would hesitate to recommend that we go ahead at this time with the development of the Kootenay. However, I do not think that is so. I also do not think the people of my riding would be too happy to go along with the idea of flooding this great area that has been built up. We realize the flooding that may come from the dam at Mica creek affects only about a dozen people at the most. That may be stretching the point a bit, but there is little habitation from Donald west to Golden and the Mica creek site. It is a large area that is uninhabited, and this flooding will cause little dislocation. We think this project should be developed separately and should be gone ahead with as soon as possible. On the other hand, I feel that the Kootenay river and the Pend d'Oreille basin integration can be proceeded with at once and give the very best return to the people of East and West Kootenay, to British Columbia and to Canada.

First, I should like to say that I am in almost complete agreement with the hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Byrne) in saying that the Kootenay river system and

speechtext:
I was agreeing. For once I agree with you. The international complications that arise when we start interfering with the natural flow of rivers might have very serious consequences and delay the development of power that is so badly and urgently needed.
To me it was a source of pleasure to hear our Prime Minister announce in the house recently, after his return from Washington, that this matter had been discussed with the top level authorities there and that arrangements had been made for future conferences. I am very glad to know that our own Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources will be in Victoria for a conference with the British Columbia government next week. I am sure that much good will come from that conference. Then we understand that in the fall there is to be another conference to deal with downstream benefits. Of course that is the crux of the whole problem of the development of power on these international streams. I wish the greatest amount of success to the minister in his meeting with the British Columbia officials in Victoria and at the conference to be held this fall.
Now, I have here the last issue of the Revelstoke Review, a newspaper which is greatly interested in the Mica creek dam which will use the water of the Columbia river for power purposes. There are some important headlines in this newspaper. One of the first is, "General McNaughton confirms feasibility of dam site." He is referring to the Mica creek dam, and I think many months ago most of us were well aware of the fact it was a feasible site. The only comment I would make is that the length of time it has taken to put this decision before the people has been unduly long and has delayed this project to some extent.
Then there is another headline which reads, "B.C. Electric plans Mica dam construction". Now, the British Columbia Electric, we understand, are deeply interested in the development of the Columbia by means of a dam at Mica creek. They are planning a dam that will be some 700 feet high and will be capable of developing 1 [DOT] 5 million horsepower, at a cost in the neighbourhood of $247 million. The power from that dam will be distributed chiefly to the lower mainland of British


Columbia over a power line 450 miles in length which will cost in the neighbourhood of $45 million or $50 million. You can see that there is a lot of money going to be tied up in this one project. However, there does not seem to be any question about the problem of financing in so far as British Columbia Electric are concerned. They claim that immediately the signal is definitely given to go ahead, they will be ready.
Before they can get that signal they have to clear five different hurdles. The first is the British Columbia government and compliance with the provisions of their water act; second, the federal government and compliance with the provisions of the International River Improvements Act; then the British Columbia public utilities commission; the United States government and the international joint commission. As I said earlier we hope, as a result of the conferences we understand are being arranged, these will present no serious obstacles.
Apparently the British Columbia Electric are prepared, immediately they receive the go ahead signal, to start exploratory engineering work which will take an estimated two years. Then a further eight years will be needed to complete the project. That is one plan that is being presented to the people of British Columbia through private enterprise, a local Canadian company. It might not be so "local" because it has ramifications from one end of Canada to the other, but it is a strictly Canadian company.
There is one other plan which I think might be worth mentioning at this time and which might command some attention from the people in this house. I have a lot of confidence, more so than possibly some other members who have spoken, in the government of British Columbia. The premier of that province has outlined a plan for the development at Mica creek. Under this plan the dam would be built by the United States with United States capital. Now, I do not want you all to get excited and say, "Here we are selling out to the Yankees". I do not think that is the idea. The United States would build this dam but the entire power developed at the dam site would be the sole property of British Columbia to do with as they saw fit. In return for control of the water flow on the Columbia river, which would result from the construction of the dam and which would allow a steadier development of power south of the border, the United States would pay the cost of the dam. In addition to that they would deliver to the British Columbia government, at the Canadian border, 20 per cent of the extra power which would be generated downstream as a result of this controlled flow.

I am not going to get into any arguments about the pros and cons of the various methods of developing the Columbia river. I am, and always will be, of course, a strong believer in private enterprise. As long as private enterprise is prepared to develop the river, I am certainly prepared to go along with them. We have these two plans; one where a Canadian company would develop it, and of course in that case the Canadian people, the users of the power generated at the dam, would have to pay for the cost of the dam. Then we have the plan of Premier Bennett whereby United States capital would build the dam, turn over the power to the people of British Columbia, and pay for the control of the river which that would give with 20 per cent of the extra power they would develop downstream. I say I am not entering into any argument on the pros and cons of these different methods at this time.
In closing, Mr. Chairman, I can only reiterate the hope that the forthcoming conference of the minister in Victoria will be successful and worthwhile. We hope that the serious problems connected with Columbia river development will be settled around the conference table.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to change the subject. I presume the discussion is over on this particular matter. I rise at this time to protest the increase in freight rates that will take place on July 3 unless something is done about it.
We have had a great many increases in freight rates since the end of the war. We have had one freight rate increase after another, until the increases before this most recent order amounted to a total of some 98 per cent. I do not think a good case has been made for an increase in freight rates. If one examines the financial position of the Canadian Pacific Railway I do not think he will find that the Canadian Pacific Railway can prove it is unable, in its present financial position, to absorb out of profits the increase in wages that has recently been granted to the railway employees. The railway workers were given an increase of some 11 per cent, but the railway company, following the award allowing the workers that increase of 11 per cent in wages, applied for a 15 per cent increase in freight rates. It is obvious that the amount of money used by the railways to pay wages is only a part of their operating costs. If they are to get a 15 per cent increase in freight rates on a very substantial part of their revenue traffic they will be getting more than has been given to the railway workers.
In recent years the Canadian Pacific Railway has shown very little change in its gross

Freight Rates
earnings. But while its gross earnings have not varied appreciably, its net earnings have been increasing. That, of course, is a natural thing when one takes into account the fact that the railway companies have been increasing their efficiency in recent years. The railway companies have been following a modernization program. They have been dieselizing their lines; they have been laying off thousands of workers; they have made tremendous savings in their wage bills, so that while gross earnings of the Canadian Pacific Railway in 1955 were $448 million, somewhat less than the gross earnings of $457 million in 1952, their net earnings on railway operations had increased from $28 [DOT] 9 million to $37 [DOT] 3 million. I think the railway companies, because of the savings they have already made, are in a financial position to pay the increases in wages that have been granted without any increase in general freight rates.
A number of briefs have been presented to the board of transport commissioners objecting to any increase in freight rates. A brief was presented by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture and one by the Saskatchewan wheat pool. In those briefs they pointed out the position agriculture faces in relation to increased freight rates. The net income of the agricultural industry has been going down in recent years and they have said that an increase in freight rates will further reduce agricultural net income; that the farm industry, unlike any other industry, is unable to pass on its increased costs. Therefore the effect of an increase in freight rates will be a further decrease in the net income of the agricultural industry.
I agree with them when they ask that whatever increase in freight rates may be granted should not be applied to primary production of this country. One might extend that argument to primary production other than farm products, to forest products, perhaps, and certain other products. But as far as agriculture is concerned I certainly agree that the increase should not affect agricultural products.
As the cost of living goes up, as labour efficiency increases, I think the trade union movements are perfectly justified in asking for periodic increases in order that the labouring man can have his fair share of the increased productivity in this country. Labour has been able to increase its standard of living, though perhaps not as rapidly as it thinks it deserves, and for that I am glad. Industry has been able to add to its prices sufficient to cover any increased costs, sufficient to have a substantial profit, a growing profit; but in this same period of time the net income of the agricultural industry has been

on the decline. This increase will add further to the decline. In a table in its brief at page 13 the Canadian Federation of Agriculture points out that the net income of the agricultural industry, in terms of 1955 dollars, fell from $1,700 million in 1949 to $1,189 million in 1955.
The Canadian Pacific Railway is not content with the 7 per cent increase that it is about to be granted. It has asked for a 15 per cent increase. The Canadian Pacific Railway is not content with a 15 per cent increase only because the company has put on a very direct campaign to get rid of the Crowsnest pass rates on grain. It is admitted that if the Crowsnest pass rates were abolished, and if the railway companies applied the same rates to the movement of grain that they apply to other commodities of similar bulk, but not necessarily of a similar value, it would increase the revenue they get for moving a bushel of wheat from 12 cents to 36 cents. In other words, if the Canadian Pacific Railway were successful in its efforts to get rid of the Crowsnest pass agreement it would reduce the cost of wheat to the producer by 36 cents a bushel. I wish to warn the government that any move to get rid of the Crowsnest pass rates will be resisted by every farm organization in western Canada. The briefs that have been presented protesting the impending increase in freight rates will be very mild reading compared to the briefs that will be presented and the action that will be taken to protest any tampering with the Crowsnest pass rates.
I rise at this time to ask the government to disallow the impending 7 per cent award. I think the railway freight rates in this country are already too high and that if the railways can prove they need an increase-and I do not think they have proved it yet-any increased revenue they may need should be obtained by some other method. I suggest the government should look very carefully at the question of using subsidies as an alternative proposition. Of course there is already a good precedent for using subsidies with regard to the railways, because of the $7 million subsidy that is now paid annually to the railway companies for maintaining their lines in northern Ontario. I am suggesting it is most unfair that the agricultural industry be further depressed by allowing a 7 per cent increase in freight rates. Unless something is done about it, in all probability this will be followed by a further increase in freight rates, and this will depress the agricultural industry worse than at the present time.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, at the resolution stage of this particular bill it is my intention to speak but for a few moments, as I have indicated to those who are charged with expressing the points of view of the various groups in the house. This resolution, nevertheless, is an important one and asks authority to introduce a bill which will authorize the federal government to enter into agreements with the provinces of Canada to provide for contributions out of the federal treasury to be made for local unemployment assistance costs to those in need.
The details of this bill respecting unemployment assistance were worked out during the past year at a number of conferences with the provinces. There were at least, I think, six different conferences some of which, of course, were devoted to other matters but one of which was devoted exclusively to working out arrangements with the provinces, as a result of which we now have agreements with six provinces to share with them in the cost of assistance to needy individuals who may be characterized as unemployed employables or unemployed unemployables, that is persons who have been out of work or who are unable to work.
Unemployment Assistance
One of the clauses of the draft agreement provides that at the first session of parliament the government of Canada will seek authority to validate the agreements that have been signed with the six provinces which I shall enumerate, these provinces being Newfoundland, British Columbia, New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island, Saskatchewan and Manitoba. Other provinces are giving consideration to the matter and at least one other is very close to signature.
The legislation which will follow upon the approval of this resolution will accomplish the following. It will provide the necessary authority for the federal government, through the Minister of National Health and Welfare, to make agreements with the provinces for sharing unemployment assistance costs. Second, it will establish the basis of the federal contribution and will specify certain types of costs which may be included and certain costs which may not be included in the reimbursement claims submitted to the federal government. On all these matters, of course, the legislative provisions will conform with those set out in the agreements already signed with the six provinces, which were tabled in this house several months ago. Third, it will authorize these agreements to be given retroactive effect for a maximum period of one year, not back beyond a period of 12 months, so that in the case of those provinces with whom agreements have been finalized they will date back to July 1, 1955. Fourth, it will ratify and confirm any agreement already made prior to the passage of the bill itself; and finally it will authorize the federal share of unemployment assistance costs covered by the bill to be provided annually out of the consolidated revenue fund.
I am sure that when we get into the discussion of the bill, the discussion will perhaps take into consideration the proposals that were made by the federal government in 1945, and likewise recommendations that were made by a royal commission whose report was discussed at the dominion-provincial conference of 1941. I can only say that the provisions of the bill to be based upon this resolution will be found to go much further than the recommendations of the Rowell-Sirois commission, and further than the proposals made in 1945. These later proposals did not include unemployables, as does this measure, and the resolutions of 1945 did not cover special cases or local situations, as does this one. The proposals of 1945 did not cover the selfemployed, and particularly they did not cover, within a certain context, fishermen and farmers.

Under the arrangement which this resolution and the bill to be based upon it envisage, which has already been endorsed by six provinces and is still under consideration by the others, I think I can say we will be able to write "finis" to the deadlock which has existed in this country for a decade or more on the subject of the responsibility of the several governmental jurisdictions for what we call residual assistance, and that henceforth there will be an assurance of organized assistance to persons in need in any part of Canada who cannot qualify for help under any of the existing social welfare measures such as unemployment insurance, supplementary benefits, old age assistance, disability pensions and so on. By this legislation we will eliminate the obstacle presented in the past by the fact that each jurisdiction has argued that responsibility belonged to another level of government. Now no excuse will exist for denying assistance to those in need in any province which has entered into an agreement with the federal government.
I believe this resolution constitutes a piece of important legislation which in its general context will win a wide measure of approval from most hon. members of this house and I am sure by those needy people in our country who have sometimes been made the victims, unwittingly perhaps, of governments which have sought to shift responsibility to other jurisdictions. I do not propose to say any more at this time in introducing this resolution. I am sure that as soon as we go into an examination of the bill we shall find there the greatest opportunity for fruitful discussion in respect of a measure which I think will win wide support.

The real fact is that a careful reading of the minutes of that conference will show that the federal government did not agree to assume entire responsibility, in the proposals which were part of the package deal, for the unemployed employables. All the federal government did was to agree to assume responsibility for this group for a limited

I think we all felt-and certainly when we had a temporary period of unemployment about a year and a half ago-that it was unfortunate that in a federal state a situation should be created whereby needy individuals should go without assistance from the community in one form or another, simply because it had not been settled which jurisdiction was either constitutionally responsible or responsible because of the lack of agreement among the various levels of government.

Would it be considered at any time that a man 40 years of age is unemployable? These people cannot get jobs; they are not considered employable in the eyes of the managers of those companies to which they apply. They are unemployable.
This is a situation we must recognize. It is happening all across the country. The situation exists in my own riding. These people simply cannot move out of the town in which they live. There is no possibility of them getting jobs. They have tried very hard to get jobs. Whenever they apply for a job they are asked, "How old are you?" If they are 40 years of age they are told, "We do not want you in our firm because you do not fit into the pension plan, and we like to train our own men". Therefore to all intents and purposes, no matter how we regard it, they are still unemployables.
This is a situation we should recognize, and something should be done for these people. Their unemployfent insurance ran out on May 1. They are quite without funds except what they saved from their earnings. At the same time, as I suggested before, they are unemployable by reason of the fact that no firm will employ them. If they go to the unemployment insurance people they might be offered other jobs, but you cannot ask a man to go out and do work on a highway or do other forms of labour when he has been a factory man all his life, or perhaps an expert mechanic. It just does not work out that way.
At the present time the situation exists, and I again call it to the attention of the government. I asked the Minister of Labour about it the other day and I now appeal to the Minister of National Health and Welfare to do something for these people.
