speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in introducing the estimates of the Department of Defence Production I would like to deal in general terms with Canada's defence production program which the department administers, in order to illustrate the scope of the work undertaken. From a defence production standpoint Canada has accomplished much in the last five years and developments have taken place which have strengthened and broadened our defence potential. In a number of fields new sources of supply have been developed in this country, and it is of interest to note that whereas in 1951 some 25 per cent of our defence orders, in dollar terms, were placed in the United States, last year this figure had dropped to 2 per ceht.

An important factor in defence production is the state of the economy as a whole, and in this regard Canada has been most fortunate. Our industrial expansion and economic growth over the past years have added immeasurably to our defensive strength. Now that the initial build-up of the defence program has been completed, and re-equipment of our forces and maintenance of our defence production base have become the major considerations in the program, the underlying strength of the Canadian economy is of vital importance. It is against this background that the present program should be considered.
In carrying out its task of filling the defence requirements of Canada's armed forces, the Department of Defence Production has maintained a flexible production program which has been adjusted to changes in these requirements over the past five years. While this year's estimates of defence expenditures for equipment and services to be supplied by this department show little change, there are a number of adjustments and adaptations which I would like to discuss today, with some reference to the effect on the program of Canadian industry.
Five years ago I pointed out that there were certain phases of aircraft production in which it was felt that this country could make a contribution, not only to our own defence effort but to that of our allies as well. In some cases this meant using design and technical know-how of other countries and adapting them, where necessary, to our own needs. In 1951 deliveries of CF-100 all-weather interceptors and Orenda engines were just about to start, the F-86 Sabre was in quantity production powered by J-47 engines purchased in the United States, the Harvard trainer program was developing and there were plans for the production of the T-33 jet trainer.
Since then we have spent almost $2 billion on the aircraft program, more than three-quarters of it in Canada, and the tasks which were outlined in 1951 have been largely completed. A great number of CF-100 fighters have been produced, the majority being of the improved mark IV model, and further improvements are still being made. Canada has produced a very successful combination of the F-86 airframe and Orenda engine. The Harvard program has been completed and the Canadian manufacturer is now the sole source of supply for maintenance parts for this widely used training aircraft. The T-33 program has also been completed and current production is limited to replacement needs only.
During the same period we have for the first time established Canada as a producer of aero engines. The outstanding achievement, of
Supply-Defence Production course, has been the Orenda, of which improved versions are now being delivered. Rolls-Royce have completed production in their Canadian plant of Nene engines for the T-33 trainers, and the product has given excellent performance. In addition, a piston engine plant has been established near Montreal by Canadian Pratt and Whitney Limited which has supplied Wasp engines for both the Canadian and the United States governments and for supply under the Canadian mutual aid program to our NATO allies.
The production record of the past five years has borne out our expectation that a Canadian aircraft industry could successfully compete in certain fields with producers in other countries. The best evidence of this fact lies in the proven performance of the product. In the Orenda-powered F-86 Sabre, the Royal Canadian Air Force possess a day interceptor which is the equal of any in regular squadron service. The CF-100 continues to be one of the mainstays of the North American continental defence system, and will shortly make its appearance in Europe as part of the Canadian air division overseas. The success of this aircraft has demonstrated Canada's ability not only to build but also to design a first-class high performance aircraft. The same is true of the Orenda jet engine, which is so largely responsible for the excellent performance which the CF-100 and Sabre have given. At the same time, the Canadian aircraft industry has proven its ability to organize these complex production tasks quickly and to deliver at reasonable costs.
With respect to costs, we are satisfied that the decision to develop Canadian production has been justified economically. For various reasons, direct cost comparisons between countries are difficult to make. No two aircraft are identical and the types produced in Canada have been designed or modified to meet characteristic Canadian requirements. In addition, the size of the production run, which for Canadian requirements is bound to be limited compared with production runs in some other countries, has an obvious bearing on the element of overhead which must be borne by each aircraft produced. The record indicates, however, that the prices we have paid compare favourably with those we would have been required to pay for aircraft produced elsewhere.
But there is more than economic advantage to consider. A direct by-product of this policy is that we now have research and production facilities and engineering experience that did not exist in Canada before.
